explanation: The condition "from Grade 10" restricts attention to that column, whose total is $90$.
Within Grade 10, $35$ students take the bus.

alternativeExplanations.title: Three denominators, three different answers
steps: Out of all students: $\dfrac{35}{200} = 0.175$.
Out of all bus riders: $\dfrac{35}{80} = 0.4375$.
Out of Grade 10: $\dfrac{35}{90} \approx 0.39$ ✓ — same numerator every time. The phrase after "from" or "of those who" names the denominator.

prompt: A scatterplot relates the number of years since a tree was planted, $x$, to its height in feet, $y$. The line of best fit is $y = 1.8x + 4$. What does $1.8$ represent in this model?

choices.label: The height of the tree when it was planted
The predicted increase in height, in feet, per year
The total height of the tree after one year
The number of years for the tree to reach $1.8$ feet

hint: The slope is a rate: output units per input unit.

hints.text: The slope is a rate: output units per input unit.
Here that is feet per year.
$1.8$ is the predicted growth in feet for each additional year.

learningObjective: Interpret the slope of a line of best fit in context.
explanation: The slope of any linear model is the change in $y$ for a one-unit change in $x$.
With $y$ in feet and $x$ in years, the slope is measured in feet per year: the tree grows about $1.8$ feet each year.
Choice A describes the intercept ($4$ feet at planting). Choice C would be $1.8 + 4 = 5.8$ feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Say the units out loud
steps: Slope units are always "$y$-units per $x$-unit" — here, feet per year.
Once you have said "feet per year", only one answer choice can match.
This works on every interpretation question in this area, and it takes about three seconds.

prompt: A researcher randomly selected $200$ students from Lincoln High School and found that $62\%$ preferred a later start time. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: About $62\%$ of all high school students nationwide prefer a later start time
About $62\%$ of students at Lincoln High School prefer a later start time
A later start time causes students to perform better
Exactly $62\%$ of students at Lincoln High School prefer a later start time

hint: A sample can only speak for the population it was drawn from.

hints.text: A sample can only speak for the population it was drawn from.
The sample came from one school, so the conclusion covers that school.
About $62\%$ of Lincoln High School students — an estimate, not an exact figure.

learningObjective: Determine the population a random sample supports conclusions about.
explanation: The students were randomly selected from Lincoln High School, so that school is the population the sample represents.
Choice A over-generalizes to a population never sampled. Choice C claims causation, which requires a controlled experiment with random assignment.
Choice D says "exactly", but a sample gives an estimate with uncertainty, not an exact population value. Choice B — "about", and scoped to the right population — is correct.

alternativeExplanations.title: Two questions settle every inference item
steps: First: who was sampled? The conclusion may not extend beyond that group.
Second: was there random *assignment* to treatments? Without it you cannot claim cause.
Random selection buys generalization; random assignment buys causation. They are different, and no study gets one for free from the other.

prompt: A poll estimates that $48\%$ of voters support a measure, with a margin of error of $3$ percentage points. Which value of the true population percentage is NOT consistent with this result?
hint: The margin of error creates an interval around the estimate.

hints.text: The margin of error creates an interval around the estimate.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easy interval: an estimate of $50\%$ with a margin of $2$ points spans $48\%$ to $52\%$. Build the interval first, then check which value sits outside it.
The interval is $48 \pm 3$, so from $45\%$ to $51\%$.
$53\%$ falls outside that interval.

learningObjective: Build and use a margin-of-error interval.
explanation: The estimate plus or minus the margin gives the plausible interval: $48 - 3 = 45$ to $48 + 3 = 51$.
Choices A, B, and C all lie within $[45, 51]$ and are therefore consistent with the poll.
$53\%$ lies outside, so it is not supported.

alternativeExplanations.title: What shrinks the margin
steps: A larger sample narrows the margin of error; a smaller one widens it.
The margin reflects sampling variability only — it does not account for a biased sampling method.
A badly-drawn sample can have a tiny margin of error and still be completely wrong about the population.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 45% looks suspicious because it sits exactly on the boundary — but the interval INCLUDES its endpoints.
Build the interval first: 45 to 51, endpoints in. Only then scan the choices for the value outside; 53% is the lone stranger.

prompt: In a study, $300$ volunteers were randomly assigned to either a new exercise program or no program. Those in the program showed significantly lower resting heart rates. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: The exercise program likely caused the lower heart rates among these volunteers
The exercise program lowers heart rates for all adults
Lower heart rates cause people to exercise more
No conclusion about cause can be drawn from this study

hint: The volunteers were *randomly assigned* to the groups. What does that permit?

hints.text: The volunteers were *randomly assigned* to the groups. What does that permit?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try the contrast: a survey asking who already exercises can only show an association, but randomly assigning people to exercise or not can show cause. The design decides what you may claim.
Random assignment to treatments allows a causal conclusion.
But the volunteers were not randomly selected from all adults, so the conclusion stays with them.

learningObjective: Distinguish what random assignment and random selection each justify.
explanation: Random *assignment* to treatment groups controls for confounding variables, so a causal claim is justified — that is what makes this an experiment rather than an observational study.
But the participants were volunteers, not a random sample of all adults, so the result cannot be generalized beyond them. That rules out choice B.
Choice C reverses the direction the design established, and choice D wrongly denies that random assignment supports causation.

alternativeExplanations.title: The two-by-two that answers every one of these
steps: Random selection + random assignment: cause, generalizable to the whole population.
Random assignment only (volunteers): cause, but only for the participants — this study.
Random selection only (survey): generalizable, but association only, never cause. Neither: association among participants only.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice B feels generous and reasonable — and it quietly extends the finding to millions of adults who were never sampled.
Volunteers were randomly ASSIGNED, not randomly SELECTED. Assignment buys the causal claim; only selection would buy the generalization.

prompt: Using the commuting table, what percent of the students who take the bus are in Grade $9$? Round to the nearest whole percent.
hint: "Of the students who take the bus" names the denominator.

hints.text: "Of the students who take the bus" names the denominator.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a two-by-two table: if $6$ of $10$ bus riders are in Grade 9, that is $60\%$ — denominator $10$, the bus total. The phrase after 'of' names the denominator.
The Bus row totals $80$, and $45$ of those are in Grade 9.

learningObjective: Compute a row-conditional percentage from a two-way table.
explanation: The phrase "of the students who take the bus" restricts the pool to the Bus row, total $80$.
Of those, $45$ are in Grade 9.
$\dfrac{45}{80} = 0.5625$, which rounds to $56\%$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Row condition versus column condition
steps: This question conditions on a *row* (bus riders), so the row total is the denominator.
The earlier question conditioned on a *column* (Grade 10), so the column total was the denominator.
Same table, same numerator style, entirely different answers. Reading which way the condition runs is the whole skill.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 45/110 ≈ 41% answers a different question — 'of Grade 9, what share ride the bus' — by conditioning on the column.
The phrase 'of the students who take the bus' names the ROW as the denominator: 45 of 80. Circle the denominator group before reading any number.

prompt: Using the commuting table, how many more Grade $9$ students than Grade $10$ students do NOT take the bus?
hint: "Not the bus" means walk plus car — or the column total minus the bus count.

hints.text: "Not the bus" means walk plus car — or the column total minus the bus count.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try it small: if a column totals $20$ and $8$ of them ride the bus, then $12$ do not. Subtracting from the column total is faster than adding the other rows.

learningObjective: Combine complement and comparison steps on a two-way table.
explanation: Grade 9 students not taking the bus: $110 - 45 = 65$ (equivalently $30 + 35$).
Grade 10 students not taking the bus: $90 - 35 = 55$ (equivalently $20 + 35$).
The difference is $65 - 55 = 10$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Subtracting from the total beats adding rows
steps: Adding $30 + 35$ works, but with four or five commute categories the complement is much faster.
Column total minus the excluded row gives the "not" count in one step.
The complement also generalizes: for probability, $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$ is the same idea.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Adding rows you did not need, or answering 65 (one grade's count) instead of the difference, are the designed exits.
Complement per column first — 110 − 45 and 90 − 35 — then subtract. Two clean complements beat three additions.

prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure $40°$ and $65°$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the third angle?
hint: The three angles of any triangle add to $180°$.

hints.text: The three angles of any triangle add to $180°$.

learningObjective: Apply the triangle angle sum.
explanation: The interior angles of a triangle always sum to $180°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: The sum never changes
steps: It is $180°$ for every triangle — acute, right, obtuse, large or small.
This is the single most-used fact in SAT geometry, and it is not on the reference sheet.
Any question giving you two angles of a triangle is handing you the third for free.

prompt: Two angles are supplementary. One measures $118°$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the other?
hint: Supplementary angles sum to $180°$.

hints.text: Supplementary angles sum to $180°$.
$62$ degrees.

learningObjective: Apply the supplementary-angle relationship.
explanation: Supplementary angles add to $180°$ — they form a straight line.
Complementary angles, by contrast, add to $90°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Keeping the two words apart
steps: Complementary comes before supplementary alphabetically, and $90$ comes before $180$ numerically.
That ordering is enough to keep them straight under time pressure.
Choosing the wrong one here gives $-28$, which is obviously impossible — so a quick plausibility check catches the mix-up too.

prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the eight angles formed measures $115°$. What is the measure, in degrees, of an angle that is supplementary to it?
hint: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, every angle is either equal to $115°$ or supplementary to it.

hints.text: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, every angle is either equal to $115°$ or supplementary to it.
The supplementary partner satisfies $115 + x = 180$.
$x = 65$ degrees.

learningObjective: Use the two-angle structure formed by a transversal across parallel lines.
explanation: A transversal crossing two parallel lines creates only two distinct angle measures, and they are supplementary.
One is $115°$, so the other is $180 - 115 = 65°$.
Four of the eight angles measure $115°$ and the other four measure $65°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Only two numbers exist in the figure
steps: Rather than memorizing "corresponding", "alternate interior", and "co-interior" separately, notice that every angle is one of just two values.
Angles that look equal are equal; angles that look different are supplementary.
With parallel lines, the picture is reliable in exactly this one respect — and it collapses eight angle names into one idea.

prompt: In a triangle, the two angles not adjacent to a certain exterior angle measure $50°$ and $70°$. What is the measure, in degrees, of that exterior angle?
hint: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

hints.text: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
$120$ degrees.

learningObjective: Apply the exterior angle theorem.
explanation: The Exterior Angle Theorem: an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent (remote) interior angles.
Check the long way: the third interior angle is $180 - 120 = 60°$, and its exterior partner is $180 - 60 = 120°$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the shortcut works
steps: The exterior angle is supplementary to its adjacent interior angle: exterior $= 180 - $ adjacent.
The three interior angles sum to $180$, so $180 - $ adjacent $=$ the other two added together.
The theorem is just those two facts combined — which is why you can always fall back on the long route if you forget it.

prompt: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two congruent sides measures $40°$. What is the measure, in degrees, of each base angle?
hint: The two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.

hints.text: The two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
They share the remaining $180 - 40 = 140$ degrees.
$140 \div 2 = 70$ degrees each.

learningObjective: Combine the isosceles base-angle property with the triangle sum.
explanation: In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the two congruent sides are equal — these are the base angles.
The vertex angle is $40°$, leaving $180 - 40 = 140°$ split evenly between them.
Each base angle is $140 \div 2 = 70°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Equal sides face equal angles
steps: The rule runs both ways: equal sides mean equal opposite angles, and equal angles mean equal opposite sides.
Locate which sides are marked congruent, then look *across* from each to find the equal angles.
Getting the vertex and base angles backwards gives $(180 - 70)/2 = 55$, and that will be an answer choice.

prompt: What is the sum, in degrees, of the interior angles of a pentagon?
hint: The formula is $(n - 2) \times 180°$ for an $n$-sided polygon.

hints.text: The formula is $(n - 2) \times 180°$ for an $n$-sided polygon.
A pentagon has $n = 5$, so $(5 - 2) \times 180$.
$3 \times 180 = 540$ degrees.

learningObjective: Apply the polygon interior-angle-sum formula.
explanation: An $n$-sided polygon splits into $n - 2$ triangles, each contributing $180°$.
For a pentagon: $(5 - 2) \times 180 = 3 \times 180 = 540°$.
If the pentagon is regular, each angle is $540 \div 5 = 108°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Derive it rather than memorize it
steps: Pick one vertex and draw diagonals to every non-adjacent vertex.
A pentagon splits into exactly $3$ triangles this way, which is where the $n - 2$ comes from.
If you blank on the formula, drawing the triangles rebuilds it in ten seconds.

prompt: The measures of the three angles of a triangle are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the largest angle?
hint: Call the angles $x$, $2x$, and $3x$.

hints.text: Call the angles $x$, $2x$, and $3x$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easier ratio: angles in the ratio $1 : 1 : 2$ give $4x = 180$, so $x = 45$ and the angles are $45$, $45$, $90$. Add the ratio parts, then divide $180$ among them.
Their sum is $6x = 180$.
$x = 30$, so the largest angle is $3(30) = 90$ degrees.

learningObjective: Use a ratio together with the triangle angle sum.
explanation: Let the angles be $x$, $2x$, and $3x$.
Their sum is $180$: $x + 2x + 3x = 6x = 180$, so $x = 30$.
The angles are $30°$, $60°$, and $90°$ — the largest is $90°$, so this is a right triangle.

alternativeExplanations.title: Ratio parts split the total
steps: The ratio $1 : 2 : 3$ has $6$ parts in total, and those parts share $180°$.
Each part is $180 \div 6 = 30°$, so the angles are $30$, $60$, and $90$.
This "total parts" method works for any ratio question — angles, money, or ingredients.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: x = 30 is the solved variable, offered as if it were an angle; the LARGEST angle is 3x.
Ratio problems end with a translation step: parts back into quantities. The answer is 3(30) = 90 degrees, and the check 30+60+90 = 180 seals it.

prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle measures $(3x + 10)°$ and the corresponding angle measures $(5x - 30)°$. What is the value of $x$?
hint: Corresponding angles formed by a transversal across parallel lines are equal.

hints.text: Corresponding angles formed by a transversal across parallel lines are equal.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try easier expressions: if corresponding angles are $(x + 20)°$ and $(2x)°$, then $x + 20 = 2x$ and $x = 20$. Congruent angles means set the expressions equal.

learningObjective: Set up an equation from an angle relationship in a parallel-line figure.
explanation: Corresponding angles are congruent when the lines are parallel, so set the expressions equal: $3x + 10 = 5x - 30$.
Subtract $3x$ and add $30$: $40 = 2x$.
$x = 20$. Check: both angles measure $70°$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: Equal or supplementary decides the equation
steps: If the angles are congruent (corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, vertical), set the expressions equal.
If they are supplementary (co-interior, or a linear pair), set the sum to $180$.
Identifying which relationship applies is the whole question — the algebra afterwards is routine.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Setting the sum to 180 — treating corresponding angles as supplementary — gives x = 25, a clean wrong answer.
Corresponding angles are CONGRUENT, so the expressions are set equal. Decide equal-or-supplementary from the angle relationship before writing the equation.

prompt: Which set of side lengths could NOT form a triangle?
hint: The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest side.

hints.text: The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest side.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an obvious failure: $1$, $2$, and $9$ cannot close, since $1 + 2 = 3 < 9$. Compare the two shortest sides against the longest — that one check is enough.
For choice B: is $3 + 4$ greater than $8$?
$3 + 4 = 7 < 8$, so those lengths cannot close into a triangle.

learningObjective: Apply the triangle inequality.
explanation: The Triangle Inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. In practice, just check the two shortest against the longest.
Only choice B fails.

alternativeExplanations.title: Picture the two short sides swinging shut
steps: Imagine the two shorter sides as hinged arms attached to the ends of the longest side.
If they are too short to meet in the middle, no triangle exists — they cannot reach across.
Checking the two shortest against the longest is sufficient; the other two comparisons are then automatic.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Testing the wrong pair — say 4 + 8 against 3 — passes everything and finds no failure.
The only test that matters: the two SHORTEST sides against the longest. If that pair fails, the triangle is impossible; if it passes, all pairs pass.

prompt: The angles of a triangle measure $(2x)°$, $(3x + 10)°$, and $(x - 10)°$. What is the value of $x$?
hint: Set the sum of the three expressions equal to $180$.

hints.text: Set the sum of the three expressions equal to $180$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try simpler expressions: angles $x$, $x$, and $x$ give $3x = 180$, so $x = 60$. Sum all three expressions, set the total to $180$, and solve.
The constants cancel: $6x = 180$, so $x = 30$.

learningObjective: Solve for a variable using the triangle angle sum.
explanation: The three angles sum to $180°$: $2x + 3x + 10 + x - 10 = 180$.
Combine like terms — the $+10$ and $-10$ cancel: $6x = 180$.
$x = 30$. The angles are $60°$, $100°$, and $20°$, which do sum to $180$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: Finish by checking, not by stopping
steps: The question asked for $x$, which is $30$ — not for an angle measure.
But computing the three angles anyway is a fast, complete verification.
If they had not summed to $180$, you would know immediately that the algebra went wrong.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 60 — the first angle, 2x — is the offered near-miss for anyone who forgets what was asked.
The question wants x itself. Solve, then re-read the stem; computing all three angles as a check also reminds you which quantity to report.

prompt: A triangle has a base of $12$ and a height of $5$. What is its area?
hint: Area of a triangle is half the base times the height.

hints.text: Area of a triangle is half the base times the height.

learningObjective: Compute the area of a triangle.
explanation: Forgetting the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ gives $60$, which is the area of the surrounding rectangle — and an answer choice.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the one-half is there
steps: Any triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height.
Draw the rectangle around it and the halving becomes obvious rather than memorized.
This also explains why the height must be perpendicular to the base — it is the side of that rectangle.

prompt: A rectangular prism has dimensions $4$ by $5$ by $6$. What is its volume?
hint: Volume of a rectangular prism is length times width times height.

hints.text: Volume of a rectangular prism is length times width times height.
$4 \times 5 \times 6$.

learningObjective: Compute the volume of a rectangular prism.
explanation: Volume $= \ell wh = 4 \times 5 \times 6 = 120$.
Equivalently: one layer holds $4 \times 5 = 20$ unit cubes, and there are $6$ layers.
The order of multiplication does not matter.

alternativeExplanations.title: Volume versus surface area
steps: Volume is what fits inside, measured in cubic units.
Surface area is the wrapping, measured in square units — here it would be $2(20 + 24 + 30) = 148$.
The units in the answer choices often tell you which one is wanted, so read them.

prompt: What is the area of a circle with radius $6$?
hint: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$.

hints.text: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$.

learningObjective: Compute the area of a circle from its radius.
explanation: Choice A, $12\pi$, is the *circumference* ($2\pi r$) — the classic mix-up.
Choice D squares the diameter instead of the radius.

alternativeExplanations.title: Area squares, circumference does not
steps: Area $= \pi r^2$ has an exponent, so the answer grows with the square of the radius.
Circumference $= 2\pi r$ is linear in $r$.
If a question mentions units, area is square units and circumference is plain units — another way to tell which formula is wanted.

prompt: What is the volume of a cylinder with radius $3$ and height $10$?
hint: Volume of a cylinder is the base area times the height.

hints.text: Volume of a cylinder is the base area times the height.
The base is a circle of area $\pi(3)^2 = 9\pi$.
$9\pi \times 10 = 90\pi$.

learningObjective: Compute the volume of a cylinder.
explanation: Volume $= \pi r^2 h$, which is the circular base area times the height.
Choice A forgets to square the radius; choice D squares the height instead.

alternativeExplanations.title: Every prism and cylinder follows one rule
steps: Volume $=$ base area $\times$ height, whatever the base shape is.
For a cylinder the base is a circle; for a rectangular prism it is a rectangle.
Cones and pyramids take a third of that — the $\tfrac{1}{3}$ appears exactly when the shape narrows to a point.

prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio $1 : 3$. What is the ratio of their areas?
hint: Area is a two-dimensional measure, so the scale factor applies twice.

hints.text: Area is a two-dimensional measure, so the scale factor applies twice.
The area ratio is the side ratio squared.
$3^2 = 9$, so the ratio is $1 : 9$.

learningObjective: Apply the square relationship between linear scale and area.
explanation: For similar figures with side ratio $k$, the area ratio is $k^2$ and the volume ratio is $k^3$.
Here $k = 3$, so the areas are in the ratio $1 : 3^2 = 1 : 9$.
Choice A is the trap that scales linearly; choice D uses the volume rule.

alternativeExplanations.title: Verify with an actual pair
steps: Take a triangle with base $2$ and height $2$: area $2$. Scale by $3$ to base $6$, height $6$: area $18$.
Building a concrete example takes fifteen seconds and settles the rule permanently.

prompt: A rectangular garden measures $20$ feet by $15$ feet. A square patio measuring $5$ feet on each side is built inside it. What is the area, in square feet, of the remaining garden?
hint: Find the whole area, then subtract the part that is no longer garden.

hints.text: Find the whole area, then subtract the part that is no longer garden.
Garden: $20 \times 15 = 300$. Patio: $5 \times 5 = 25$.
$300 - 25 = 275$ square feet.

learningObjective: Compute a composite area by subtraction.
explanation: Total rectangle area: $20 \times 15 = 300$ square feet.
Patio area: $5^2 = 25$ square feet.
Remaining garden: $300 - 25 = 275$ square feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Subtract the hole, do not rebuild the shape
steps: Trying to carve the remaining region into rectangles works but takes four times as long.
Whole minus hole is the standard move for any shaded-region or leftover-area question.
It also works for circles inside squares, which is the most common version on the test.

prompt: What is the volume of a sphere with radius $3$?
hint: The sphere volume formula is on the reference sheet: $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.

hints.text: The sphere volume formula is on the reference sheet: $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try radius $1$: $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(1)^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi$. Cube the radius first, then multiply by $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi$ — the exponent applies to $r$ alone.

learningObjective: Apply the sphere volume formula.
explanation: $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with $r = 3$.
Cube the radius before multiplying by the fraction — $\left(\tfrac{4}{3} \times 3\right)^3$ is a different and wrong quantity.

alternativeExplanations.title: Use the reference sheet without losing time
steps: The sphere, cone, and pyramid formulas are all provided — you do not need to memorize them.
But each lookup costs about fifteen seconds, and geometry questions cluster late in a module.
Knowing them cold converts that lookup time into checking time.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 27π drops the 4/3 entirely; another classic slip cubes 4/3·r instead of r alone.
Cube the radius first — 27 — then apply 4/3 π. Order of operations is the entire difficulty of the sphere formula.

prompt: All three dimensions of a rectangular prism are doubled. The volume of the new prism is how many times the volume of the original?
hint: Volume multiplies three lengths together, and each one doubled.

hints.text: Volume multiplies three lengths together, and each one doubled.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a unit cube: a $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cube has volume $1$; doubled to $2 \times 2 \times 2$ it has volume $8$. Each of the three dimensions contributes one factor of $2$.
$2 \times 2 \times 2$.
$8$ times.

learningObjective: Apply the cube relationship between linear scale and volume.
explanation: Volume is $\ell wh$. Doubling each of the three dimensions gives $(2\ell)(2w)(2h) = 8\ell wh$.
So the volume becomes $8$ times as large.
Concretely: a $2 \times 3 \times 4$ prism has volume $24$; doubled to $4 \times 6 \times 8$ it has volume $192 = 8 \times 24$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: The 1, 2, 3 rule
steps: Scaling lengths by $k$ multiplies lengths by $k$, areas by $k^2$, and volumes by $k^3$.
The exponent is just the number of dimensions being measured.
Doubling gives $\times 2$, $\times 4$, $\times 8$ — and the trap answer is always the one that scaled linearly.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 2 and 4 — the length and area answers — flank the correct 8 in the choices.
Volume is three-dimensional, so the factor applies three times: 2³. Match the exponent to the dimension being measured, always.

prompt: Triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$. Side $AB = 6$ corresponds to side $DE = 15$, and side $BC = 8$. What is the length of side $EF$?
hint: Find the scale factor from the pair of sides you know.

hints.text: Find the scale factor from the pair of sides you know.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easy scale: if $AB = 2$ matches $DE = 6$, the factor is $3$, so a side of $5$ becomes $15$. Find the factor from the known pair, then apply it.

learningObjective: Use a similarity scale factor to find a missing side.
explanation: Corresponding sides of similar triangles are in a constant ratio: $\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5$.
Every side of $DEF$ is $2.5$ times its partner in $ABC$.
$EF = 2.5 \times BC = 2.5 \times 8 = 20$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Set up a proportion instead
steps: $\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{BC}{EF}$, so $\dfrac{6}{15} = \dfrac{8}{EF}$.
Cross-multiply: $6 \cdot EF = 120$, so $EF = 20$.
Whichever route you take, keep the two triangles in a consistent order on both sides of the equation — mixing them up is how this question is usually lost.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Inverting the scale factor gives 8 × (6/15) = 3.2 — shrinking a triangle the problem says grew.
Decide direction first: DEF is the larger triangle, so its sides must come out LARGER. An answer smaller than 8 refutes itself.

prompt: A cone and a cylinder have the same radius and the same height. The cylinder has a volume of $60$ cubic inches. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the cone?
hint: A cone with the same base and height holds one third as much as a cylinder.

hints.text: A cone with the same base and height holds one third as much as a cylinder.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try matching solids: a cylinder of volume $30$ has a same-base same-height cone of volume $10$. The cone is always one third — no need to know $r$ or $h$.
$20$ cubic inches.

learningObjective: Relate cone and cylinder volumes with matching base and height.
explanation: Cylinder volume is $\pi r^2 h$; cone volume is $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.
With the same $r$ and $h$, the cone holds exactly one third as much.
$60 \div 3 = 20$ cubic inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Where every one-third comes from
steps: Cone-to-cylinder and pyramid-to-prism are both exactly $\tfrac{1}{3}$, given the same base and height.
The factor appears whenever a solid tapers to a single point instead of running straight up.
Recognizing this lets you answer without computing $r$ or $h$ at all — which is exactly why the question withholds them.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Multiplying by 3 gives 180 — the relationship run backwards.
The cone is the SMALLER solid: same base and height, a third of the volume. Divide, and confirm the answer is less than 60.

prompt: A right triangle has legs of length $6$ and $8$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
hint: Use $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ — or recognize a familiar triple.

hints.text: Use $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ — or recognize a familiar triple.

learningObjective: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to find a hypotenuse.
explanation: This is the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple doubled — recognizing it skips the arithmetic entirely.

alternativeExplanations.title: The triples worth memorizing
steps: $6$-$8$-$10$, $9$-$12$-$15$, and $10$-$24$-$26$ are all disguised versions of these.
Spotting one turns a square-root computation into instant recall, which matters most late in a module.

prompt: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle $\theta$ has length $3$ and the hypotenuse has length $5$. What is the value of $\sin\theta$? Give your answer as a decimal.
hint: SOH: sine is opposite over hypotenuse.

hints.text: SOH: sine is opposite over hypotenuse.
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

learningObjective: Compute a sine ratio in a right triangle.
explanation: SOH-CAH-TOA: $\sin = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$.
The third side would be $4$, making this a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle.

alternativeExplanations.title: The hypotenuse never changes; the others do
steps: The hypotenuse is always the side across from the right angle, regardless of which acute angle you are working with.
But "opposite" and "adjacent" swap when you switch from one acute angle to the other.
Label the triangle relative to the named angle *before* choosing a ratio.

prompt: A $45°$-$45°$-$90°$ triangle has legs of length $7$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
hint: The sides of a $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle are in the ratio $1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$.

hints.text: The sides of a $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle are in the ratio $1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$.
The hypotenuse is the leg times $\sqrt{2}$.

learningObjective: Apply the 45-45-90 side ratio.
explanation: In a $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle the two legs are equal and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times a leg.
So the hypotenuse is $7\sqrt{2}$.
Verify with Pythagoras: $7^2 + 7^2 = 98$, and $\sqrt{98} = 7\sqrt{2}$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: The two special triangles
steps: $45$-$45$-$90$: sides $1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$, an isosceles right triangle — half a square along its diagonal.
$30$-$60$-$90$: sides $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$, with the shortest side opposite the $30°$ — half an equilateral triangle.
Choice C uses the wrong triangle's radical, which is why both appear among the choices.

prompt: In a $30°$-$60°$-$90°$ triangle, the side opposite the $30°$ angle has length $5$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
hint: The sides are in the ratio $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$, shortest opposite the $30°$.

hints.text: The sides are in the ratio $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$, shortest opposite the $30°$.
The hypotenuse is twice the shortest side.

learningObjective: Apply the 30-60-90 side ratio.
explanation: In a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle the sides are $x$, $x\sqrt{3}$, and $2x$, with $x$ opposite the $30°$ angle.
Here $x = 5$, so the hypotenuse is $2(5) = 10$.
The remaining side, opposite the $60°$, is $5\sqrt{3}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Bigger angle, bigger opposite side
steps: In any triangle the largest angle faces the longest side.
So the $30°$ faces the shortest side and the $90°$ faces the hypotenuse — this orders the sides without memorizing which is which.
If your answer puts a long side opposite a small angle, you have matched them backwards.

prompt: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle $\theta$ has length $12$ and the side adjacent to $\theta$ has length $5$. What is the value of $\tan\theta$? Give your answer as a decimal.
hint: TOA: tangent is opposite over adjacent.

hints.text: TOA: tangent is opposite over adjacent.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{12}{5}$.

learningObjective: Compute a tangent ratio in a right triangle.
explanation: $\tan = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac{12}{5} = 2.4$.
The hypotenuse here would be $13$ — this is a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle.
Note that tangent, unlike sine and cosine, can exceed $1$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Range as a sanity check
steps: Sine and cosine are always between $-1$ and $1$, because the hypotenuse is the longest side.
Tangent has no such bound — it can be any real number.
So a sine answer above $1$ is definitely wrong, but a tangent above $1$ is perfectly ordinary.

prompt: In a right triangle, angles $A$ and $B$ are the two acute angles. If $\sin A = 0.8$, what is the value of $\cos B$?
hint: The two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.

hints.text: The two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.
And $\sin x = \cos(90° - x)$.
So $\cos B = \sin A = 0.8$.

learningObjective: Apply the complementary-angle (cofunction) identity.
explanation: The acute angles of a right triangle sum to $90°$, so $B = 90° - A$.
The cofunction identity says $\cos(90° - A) = \sin A$.
Therefore $\cos B = \sin A = 0.8$.

alternativeExplanations.title: See it in the triangle
steps: The side opposite angle $A$ is the side *adjacent* to angle $B$ — it is the same physical side.
So $\sin A$ and $\cos B$ are literally the same ratio, over the shared hypotenuse.
That is the whole content of the cofunction identity, and it is a recurring SAT question.

prompt: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of length $13$ and one leg of length $5$. What is the length of the other leg?
hint: Rearrange $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ to solve for the missing leg.

hints.text: Rearrange $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ to solve for the missing leg.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a known triple: hypotenuse $5$ with a leg of $3$ gives $\sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$. Finding a leg means subtracting, and the answer must come out smaller than the hypotenuse.

learningObjective: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to find a leg.
explanation: The hypotenuse is $c = 13$, so $5^2 + b^2 = 13^2$.
This is the $5$-$12$-$13$ triple.

alternativeExplanations.title: Subtract when finding a leg, add when finding the hypotenuse
steps: Adding here would give $\sqrt{169 + 25} \approx 13.9$ — larger than the hypotenuse, which is impossible.
The hypotenuse is always the longest side, so a leg must come out smaller than it.
That plausibility check catches the add/subtract error immediately.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Adding gives √194 ≈ 13.9 — a 'leg' longer than the hypotenuse, which is geometrically impossible.
Finding a leg means SUBTRACTING squares. The built-in check: any leg must come out shorter than 13.

prompt: In a right triangle, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$ where $\theta$ is an acute angle. What is the value of $\sin\theta$? Give your answer as a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
hint: Cosine gives you the adjacent side and the hypotenuse. Find the third side.

hints.text: Cosine gives you the adjacent side and the hypotenuse. Find the third side.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle: if $\cos\theta = \tfrac{3}{5}$, the third side is $4$, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{4}{5}$. Sketch the triangle from the ratio, then read the side you need.
Adjacent $= 5$, hypotenuse $= 13$, so the opposite side is $12$.
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{12}{13} \approx 0.92$.

learningObjective: Find one trig ratio from another using the triangle sides.
explanation: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{5}{13}$, so treat the adjacent side as $5$ and the hypotenuse as $13$.
By the Pythagorean theorem the opposite side is $\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$.
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{12}{13} \approx 0.92$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Or use the Pythagorean identity
steps: $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, so $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{13}\right)^2 = 1 - \tfrac{25}{169} = \tfrac{144}{169}$.
$\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{13}$, taking the positive root since $\theta$ is acute.
Sketching the triangle is usually faster and less error-prone, but the identity works when no triangle is described.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Re-entering 5/13 — the cosine you were given — or forming 5/12 are the two designed misses.
Sketch the triangle: adjacent 5, hypotenuse 13, so the missing opposite is 12 and sine is 12/13. The drawing keeps the three sides in their lanes.

prompt: A $20$-foot ladder leans against a wall, making a $60°$ angle with the ground. How far up the wall, in feet, does the ladder reach? Give your answer in the form $a\sqrt{3}$ by entering the value of $a$.
hint: The height up the wall is the side opposite the $60°$ angle, and the ladder is the hypotenuse.

hints.text: The height up the wall is the side opposite the $60°$ angle, and the ladder is the hypotenuse.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a smaller ladder: a $10$-foot ladder at $60°$ is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $10$, so the short side is $5$ and the height is $5\sqrt{3}$. Same triangle, half the size.
This is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $20$, so the short side is $10$.
The side opposite the $60°$ is $10\sqrt{3}$, so $a = 10$.

learningObjective: Model a real-world situation with a special right triangle.
explanation: The ladder, the wall, and the ground form a right triangle with the ladder as the hypotenuse ($20$ feet).
The ladder makes a $60°$ angle with the ground, so this is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle. The hypotenuse is $2x$, so $x = 10$.
The height up the wall is opposite the $60°$ angle, which is $x\sqrt{3} = 10\sqrt{3}$ feet. So $a = 10$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Or go straight through sine
steps: $\sin 60° = \dfrac{\text{height}}{20}$, so height $= 20\sin 60° = 20 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3}$.
Same answer, and it does not require noticing the special triangle.
Recognizing $30$-$60$-$90$ is faster; the sine route is the reliable fallback.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Entering 17.32 — the full height 10√3 as a decimal — ignores the answer-format sentence and scores zero.
The stem asks for a where the height is a√3. Formatted answers are graded on the format: re-read the final sentence before touching the keypad.

prompt: From a point on level ground $40$ feet from the base of a tree, the angle of elevation to the top of the tree is $\theta$, where $\tan\theta = 1.5$. What is the height of the tree, in feet?
hint: Tangent relates the opposite side (the height) to the adjacent side (the ground distance).

hints.text: Tangent relates the opposite side (the height) to the adjacent side (the ground distance).

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try easy numbers: if $\tan\theta = 2$ and the ground distance is $10$ feet, the height is $2 \times 10 = 20$ feet. Tangent times the adjacent side gives the opposite side.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{40} = 1.5$.
Height $= 1.5 \times 40 = 60$ feet.

learningObjective: Use tangent to solve an angle-of-elevation problem.
explanation: The tree, the ground, and the line of sight form a right triangle. The height is opposite the angle; the $40$ feet is adjacent.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac{h}{40} = 1.5$.
$h = 1.5 \times 40 = 60$ feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Tangent is the elevation ratio
steps: Angle-of-elevation and angle-of-depression problems almost always use tangent, because the two known quantities are height and horizontal distance — the two legs.
Sine and cosine appear only when the hypotenuse (the direct line of sight) is involved.
Identifying which two sides the problem hands you selects the ratio immediately.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Dividing 40 by 1.5 ≈ 26.7 treats tangent as adjacent-over-opposite — the ratio upside down.
Tangent is opposite over adjacent, and the height is the OPPOSITE side here: h = 40 × 1.5. Label the triangle before computing.

prompt: The equation of a circle is $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25$. What is the radius of the circle?
hint: In standard form the right side is $r^2$, not $r$.

hints.text: In standard form the right side is $r^2$, not $r$.

learningObjective: Read the radius from the standard form of a circle equation.
explanation: Standard form is $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$.
Answering $25$ is the trap — the right side is the radius *squared*.

alternativeExplanations.title: Two traps in one equation
steps: First: the right side is $r^2$, so take a square root.
Second: the centre signs are opposite what they appear — $(x - 3)$ means $h = 3$, and $(y + 2)$ means $k = -2$.
Nearly every circle-equation question is built on one or both of these.

prompt: What is the center of the circle $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25$?
hint: The form is $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$ with centre $(h, k)$.

hints.text: The form is $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$ with centre $(h, k)$.
The centre is $(3, -2)$.

learningObjective: Read the center from the standard form of a circle equation.
explanation: Match against $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$.
The centre is $(3, -2)$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Set each squared term to zero
steps: The centre is where both squared terms vanish, so solve $x - 3 = 0$ and $y + 2 = 0$.
That gives $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ directly, with the sign flip handled by the algebra rather than by memory.
This is the same reliable trick that reads a parabola vertex out of vertex form.

prompt: What is the circumference of a circle with radius $7$?
hint: Circumference is $2\pi r$.

hints.text: Circumference is $2\pi r$.

learningObjective: Compute a circumference from a radius.
explanation: Circumference $= 2\pi r = 2\pi(7) = 14\pi$.
Choice C, $49\pi$, is the *area* — it squares the radius instead of doubling it.
Circumference is also $\pi d$, and the diameter here is $14$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Which formula, at a glance
steps: Circumference has no exponent: $2\pi r$, or $\pi d$.
Area has the square: $\pi r^2$.
If the answer choices include both $14\pi$ and $49\pi$, the question is checking exactly this distinction.

prompt: A circle has radius $8$. What is the length of an arc with a central angle of $90°$?
hint: The arc is a fraction of the whole circumference — which fraction?

hints.text: The arc is a fraction of the whole circumference — which fraction?
$\dfrac{90}{360} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, and the circumference is $16\pi$.

learningObjective: Compute an arc length as a fraction of the circumference.
explanation: The central angle is $\dfrac{90}{360} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ of the full circle.
The full circumference is $2\pi(8) = 16\pi$.
The arc is one quarter of that: $4\pi$.

alternativeExplanations.title: One idea covers arcs and sectors both
steps: Compute the fraction $\dfrac{\text{central angle}}{360}$ once.
Multiply it by the circumference for arc length, or by the area for sector area.
Do not memorize two formulas — memorize the fraction and then pick what to multiply it by.

prompt: A circle has radius $6$. What is the area of a sector with a central angle of $60°$?
hint: Find the fraction of the circle, then take that fraction of the area.

hints.text: Find the fraction of the circle, then take that fraction of the area.
$\dfrac{60}{360} = \dfrac{1}{6}$, and the area is $36\pi$.

learningObjective: Compute a sector area as a fraction of the circle area.
explanation: The fraction of the circle is $\dfrac{60}{360} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.
The full area is $\pi r^2 = \pi(6)^2 = 36\pi$.
The sector area is $\dfrac{1}{6} \times 36\pi = 6\pi$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sector versus arc
steps: A sector is a pie slice — a two-dimensional region measured in square units.
An arc is just the curved edge — a one-dimensional length.
Here the arc would be $\tfrac{1}{6}(12\pi) = 2\pi$, which is choice A. Both appear among the choices deliberately.

prompt: What is the radian measure of an angle of $135°$?
hint: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ to convert degrees to radians.

hints.text: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ to convert degrees to radians.
Simplify by $45$: $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

learningObjective: Convert between degrees and radians.
explanation: Since $180° = \pi$ radians, multiply degrees by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$.
Simplifying gives $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Reason in quarter-turns
steps: $180°$ is $\pi$, so $90°$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $45°$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$135° = 3 \times 45°$, so it is $3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
Also a quick check: $135°$ is between $90°$ and $180°$, so the answer must be between $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\pi$ — which eliminates B and D immediately.

prompt: The equation $x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y = 12$ describes a circle. What is the radius of the circle?
hint: Complete the square in $x$ and again in $y$.

hints.text: Complete the square in $x$ and again in $y$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try one variable: $x^2 - 4x = 5$ becomes $(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 5 + 4$, so $(x - 2)^2 = 9$. Do exactly that twice — once for $x$, once for $y$ — adding to both sides each time.

learningObjective: Convert an expanded circle equation to standard form.
explanation: Group the terms: $(x^2 - 6x) + (y^2 + 4y) = 12$.
Complete each square. For $x$: half of $-6$ is $-3$, squared is $9$. For $y$: half of $4$ is $2$, squared is $4$. Add both to *each* side: $(x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4$.
That is $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25$, so the centre is $(3, -2)$ and the radius is $5$.

alternativeExplanations.title: The step people forget
steps: Whatever you add to complete a square must also be added to the right side — twice here, once for each variable.
Skipping that gives a right side of $12$ and a radius of $\sqrt{12}$, which is wrong.
Write the additions on both sides in the same motion and the error cannot happen.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Forgetting to add the 9 and 4 to the right side leaves r² = 12 and a wrong radius of about 3.46.
Whatever completes a square on the left lands on the right in the same breath — twice here, once per variable. Then r² = 25 reads off r = 5.

prompt: A circle has radius $5$. What is the length of an arc that subtends a central angle of $1.2$ radians?
hint: When the angle is in radians, arc length has a very short formula.

hints.text: When the angle is in radians, arc length has a very short formula.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try radius $1$: an angle of $2$ radians subtends an arc of $2$, since $s = r\theta = 1 \times 2$. That is the definition of a radian, which is why the formula is so short.
$s = r\theta$.

learningObjective: Use the radian arc-length formula.
explanation: For an angle measured in radians, arc length is $s = r\theta$ — no fractions of $360$ required.
This simplicity is the whole reason radians exist as a unit.

alternativeExplanations.title: The formula only works in radians
steps: With $\theta$ in degrees you must use $s = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \cdot 2\pi r$ instead.
Plugging a degree measure into $s = r\theta$ gives an answer far too large.
Check the units the question states before choosing the formula — the SAT mixes both deliberately.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Reaching for angle/360 × 2πr — the degree recipe — mangles a radian problem and produces a π that should not be there.
Radians earn the short formula: s = rθ = 5 × 1.2 = 6, no π anywhere. Check the angle's unit before choosing the recipe.

prompt: A circle has a circumference of $20\pi$. What is its area?
hint: Work back to the radius first — it is the bridge between the two formulas.

hints.text: Work back to the radius first — it is the bridge between the two formulas.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a small circle: circumference $4\pi$ gives $2\pi r = 4\pi$, so $r = 2$ and the area is $4\pi$. Route through the radius — it connects the two formulas.
$2\pi r = 20\pi$ gives $r = 10$.

learningObjective: Chain the circumference and area formulas through the radius.
explanation: From the circumference: $2\pi r = 20\pi$, so $r = 10$.
Then the area is $\pi r^2 = \pi(10)^2 = 100\pi$.
Choice C uses the diameter $20$ in place of the radius.

alternativeExplanations.title: The radius is always the middle step
steps: Any circle question that gives one measure and asks for another routes through the radius.
Circumference → radius → area, or area → radius → circumference.
Solving for $r$ first turns a two-formula question into two one-formula questions.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice C, 400π, squares the diameter 20 — the number the problem dangles — instead of the radius.
Route through the radius explicitly: 2πr = 20π forces r = 10 on paper. Once r is written down, the area formula cannot grab the wrong number.

prompt: In a circle of radius $9$, an arc has length $6\pi$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the arc's central angle?
hint: What fraction of the full circumference is this arc?

hints.text: What fraction of the full circumference is this arc?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a half circle: radius $2$ gives circumference $4\pi$, so an arc of $2\pi$ is half the circle, or $180°$. Find the fraction, then take that fraction of $360°$.
The circumference is $18\pi$, and $\dfrac{6\pi}{18\pi} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

learningObjective: Recover a central angle from an arc length.
explanation: The full circumference is $2\pi(9) = 18\pi$.
The arc is $\dfrac{6\pi}{18\pi} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ of the circle.
So the central angle is $\dfrac{1}{3} \times 360° = 120°$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Or use s = rθ and convert
steps: $6\pi = 9\theta$ gives $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians.
Convert: $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 120°$.
Both routes work. The fraction-of-the-circle method avoids the conversion, so it is usually faster when the answer is wanted in degrees.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Leaving the answer as 2π/3 ≈ 2.09 — radians in a degree box — is the final-step trap.
The stem says degrees, so the fraction-of-circle route is safest: (6π/18π) × 360 = 120. Match the unit of the answer field, not of your method.

prompt: A school survey records four things about each student. Which one is a QUANTITATIVE variable?

choices.label: Jersey number on the soccer team

hint: Quantitative means the numbers MEASURE or COUNT something, so averaging them makes sense.

hints.text: Quantitative means the numbers MEASURE or COUNT something, so averaging them makes sense.
A zip code and a jersey number are made of digits, but an "average zip code" is meaningless. They are labels.
Number of siblings is a count. An average of $1.8$ siblings makes sense, so it is quantitative: choice D.

explanation: A categorical variable sorts people into groups: lunch item, zip code and jersey number all do that, even when they use digits.
A quantitative variable counts or measures something, and arithmetic on it means something.
Number of siblings is a count, so it is quantitative. Choice D.

alternativeExplanations.title: The averaging test
steps: Ask: would an average of this variable mean anything?
Average zip code 94582.3? No. Average jersey number 11.4? No. Average favorite lunch? No.
Average number of siblings 1.8? Yes. That one is quantitative.

prompt: A bar graph shows the pets of $40$ students: dogs $16$, cats $12$, fish $7$, no pet $5$. What percent of the students have a dog?
hint: A percent compares a part with the whole group. Which number is the part here, and which is the whole?

hints.text: A percent compares a part with the whole group. Which number is the part here, and which is the whole?
The part is the $16$ dog owners and the whole is all $40$ students, so work out $\frac{16}{40}$ and turn it into a percent.
$\frac{16}{40} = 0.40$, so $40$ percent of the students have a dog.

explanation: The question asks about dog owners only, so the part is the $16$ students in the dog bar.
The whole is every student surveyed, which is $40$, so the relative frequency is $\frac{16}{40} = 0.40$.
Multiplying by $100$ turns the decimal into a percent, so $40$ percent of the students have a dog.

alternativeExplanations.title: Simplify the fraction first
steps: $\frac{16}{40}$ divides top and bottom by $8$ to give $\frac{2}{5}$.
$\frac{2}{5}$ of anything is $40$ percent — two of every five students.

prompt: Eight quiz scores are $6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10$. If you draw a dotplot, how many dots are stacked above the number $8$?
hint: A dotplot puts ONE dot per data value, stacked above that number on the line.

hints.text: A dotplot puts ONE dot per data value, stacked above that number on the line.
Count how many times $8$ appears in the list.
$8$ appears three times, so there are $3$ dots above $8$.

explanation: Each score becomes one dot above its value.
The score $8$ shows up three times in the list.
So the tallest stack, above $8$, has $3$ dots. That value is the mode.

alternativeExplanations.title: Build the whole plot
steps: Above 6: 1 dot. Above 7: 2 dots. Above 8: 3 dots.
Above 9: 1 dot. Above 10: 1 dot. Total $1 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 8$ dots, matching the 8 scores.
The stack above 8 is the tallest, with 3 dots.

prompt: A histogram of home prices in a city has most bars bunched at the lower prices and a long thin tail stretching toward a few very expensive homes. Which word describes the shape?
hint: Skew is named for the direction the TAIL points, not where the pile of data sits.

hints.text: Skew is named for the direction the TAIL points, not where the pile of data sits.
Expensive homes are large numbers, so they sit on the right side of the number line.
The tail stretches to the right, so the distribution is skewed right: choice B.

explanation: Most homes are moderately priced, so the tall bars sit on the left.
A few very expensive homes make a long tail toward the large values on the right.
The tail points right, so the shape is skewed right (choice B).

alternativeExplanations.title: Picture the mean being dragged
steps: Imagine the histogram as a seesaw balanced at the mean.
A few huge prices on the right drag the balance point to the right of the median.
When the mean is pulled right, the tail is on the right: skewed right.

prompt: The table gives the one-way commute times of $40$ employees, grouped as in a histogram. What percent of the employees commute less than $20$ minutes?
hint: Each bar covers a range of times. Decide which bars lie completely below $20$ minutes before you count anyone.

hints.text: Each bar covers a range of times. Decide which bars lie completely below $20$ minutes before you count anyone.
The $0$ to $10$ bar holds $4$ employees and the $10$ to $20$ bar holds $10$. Add those counts, then divide the sum by the total of $40$.
$4 + 10 = 14$ and $\frac{14}{40} = 0.35$, so $35$ percent of the employees commute less than $20$ minutes.

explanation: A commute under $20$ minutes falls in either the $0$ to $10$ bar or the $10$ to $20$ bar, so those are the two bars to use.
Adding their counts gives $4 + 10 = 14$ employees with a commute below $20$ minutes.
The whole group is $40$ employees, so the fraction is $\frac{14}{40} = 0.35$.
As a percent, $35$ percent of the employees commute less than $20$ minutes.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count the other side instead
steps: Employees at $20$ minutes or more: $16 + 10 = 26$, which is $\frac{26}{40} = 65$ percent.
Everyone is either under 20 or at least 20, so the rest is $100 - 65 = 35$ percent.

prompt: The stemplot shows the ages of the $10$ players on a recreational soccer team (key: $2|3$ means $23$ years). How many players are $23$ or older?
hint: In a stemplot the stem is the tens digit and each leaf is the ones digit of one player. Where in the plot does the age $23$ sit?

hints.text: In a stemplot the stem is the tens digit and each leaf is the ones digit of one player. Where in the plot does the age $23$ sit?
Written out, the ages are $12, 15, 18, 20, 23, 23, 27, 31, 34, 40$. Count every age from the first $23$ to the end of the list, and remember that $23$ itself is included.
The ages $23, 23, 27, 31, 34, 40$ qualify, so $6$ players are $23$ or older.

explanation: Read the plot row by row to recover the ages: stem $1$ gives $12, 15, 18$; stem $2$ gives $20, 23, 23, 27$; stem $3$ gives $31, 34$; stem $4$ gives $40$.
"$23$ or older" includes $23$ itself, so both leaves of $3$ on stem $2$ count, along with everything after them.
The ages that qualify are $23, 23, 27, 31, 34, 40$, which is $6$ players.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count the ones you skip
steps: Ages under 23 are $12, 15, 18, 20$ — four players.
There are 10 leaves in all, so $10 - 4 = 6$ players are 23 or older.

prompt: A two-way table sorts $120$ students by grade and whether they play a school sport. What percent of the JUNIORS play a sport?
hint: "Of the juniors" tells you the whole is the junior ROW, not all $120$ students.

hints.text: "Of the juniors" tells you the whole is the junior ROW, not all $120$ students.
Divide the juniors who play a sport by the total number of juniors: $\frac{30}{50}$.
$\frac{30}{50} = 0.60$, so $60$ percent of the juniors play a sport.

explanation: The phrase "of the juniors" sets a condition, so the whole is the junior row only, not all $120$ students.
From the table, $30$ juniors play a sport and there are $50$ juniors altogether.
The conditional relative frequency is $\frac{30}{50} = 0.60$, so $60$ percent of the juniors play a sport.

alternativeExplanations.title: Watch the wrong denominator
steps: $\frac{30}{120} = 25$ percent answers a different question: what percent of ALL students are sporty juniors.
$\frac{30}{65} \approx 46$ percent answers: what percent of athletes are juniors.
The question conditions on juniors, so the denominator must be 50, giving 60 percent.

prompt: At a small company, nine employees each earn about $\$40{,}000$ and the owner earns $\$400{,}000$. Which statement about the ten salaries is true?

choices.label: The mean is greater than the median
The mean is less than the median
The mean and the median are equal

hint: The median only cares about the MIDDLE value. The mean adds up every dollar, including the owner's.

hints.text: The median only cares about the MIDDLE value. The mean adds up every dollar, including the owner's.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $1, 1, 1, 100$. Median $= 1$. Mean $= \frac{103}{4} = 25.75$. One huge value drags the mean up but leaves the median alone. Same idea here.
The median of ten salaries is the average of the 5th and 6th values, both about $\$40{,}000$. Now compute the mean: $\frac{9(40{,}000) + 400{,}000}{10}$.
Mean $= \frac{760{,}000}{10} = \$76{,}000$, median $\approx \$40{,}000$. The mean is greater: choice A.

explanation: Sorted, the salaries are nine values near $\$40{,}000$ and one at $\$400{,}000$. The 5th and 6th values are both about $\$40{,}000$, so the median is about $\$40{,}000$.
The mean uses every dollar: $\frac{9 \times 40{,}000 + 400{,}000}{10} = \frac{760{,}000}{10}$, which is $\$76{,}000$.
The one huge salary pulls the mean far above the median, so choice A is true. (Choice D mixes up the two: $\$76{,}000$ is the mean.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Shape tells the story
steps: Nine salaries pile up on the left and one sits far to the right: skewed right.
In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the tail, so mean $>$ median.
That matches choice A without computing a thing.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice D
steps: $\$76{,}000$ is a real number from this problem, which makes D tempting.
But it is the MEAN. Nobody at the company earns anywhere near $\$76{,}000$, which is exactly why the median is the better "typical salary" here.
The median stays at about $\$40{,}000$, so D is false and A is true.

prompt: Five students from Class A scored $70, 75, 80, 85, 90$ on a test. Five students from Class B scored $60, 78, 80, 82, 100$. Which comparison is correct?

choices.label: Class B has a higher mean than Class A
The classes have the same mean and median, but Class B is more spread out
The classes have the same mean, but Class A has the higher median
Class A is more spread out because its scores change by the same amount each time

hint: Compare center first (mean and median), then spread (range or how far scores sit from the middle).

hints.text: Compare center first (mean and median), then spread (range or how far scores sit from the middle).

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: $4, 5, 6$ and $1, 5, 9$ both have mean $5$ and median $5$, but the second set is far more spread out. Same check here with five scores.
Class A: mean $= \frac{400}{5} = 80$, median $80$. Class B: mean $= \frac{400}{5} = 80$, median $80$. Now compare the ranges.
Range A $= 90 - 70 = 20$; range B $= 100 - 60 = 40$. Same center, B more spread: choice B.

explanation: Class A: $70 + 75 + 80 + 85 + 90 = 400$, so the mean is $80$; the middle value is $80$.
Class B: $60 + 78 + 80 + 82 + 100 = 400$, so the mean is also $80$; the middle value is also $80$.
Spread differs: Class A ranges $20$ points, Class B ranges $40$ points and its extreme scores sit farther from $80$. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Distances from the center
steps: Class A distances from 80: $10, 5, 0, 5, 10$ — average distance 6.
Class B distances from 80: $20, 2, 0, 2, 20$ — average distance 8.8.
Bigger typical distance means more variability, so Class B is more spread out.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why choice D is a trap
steps: Evenly spaced scores look "orderly", but spread is about how far values are from the center, not about a pattern.
Class A's farthest scores are 10 points from the middle; Class B's are 20 points away.
So Class B, not A, has the greater spread.

prompt: A histogram of $50$ runners' 5K times has these bars: $15$ to $<20$ min: $3$; $20$ to $<25$: $12$; $25$ to $<30$: $20$; $30$ to $<35$: $10$; $35$ to $<40$: $5$. Which interval must contain the median time?

choices.label: It cannot be determined from a histogram

hint: With $50$ values, the median is the average of the 25th and 26th times in order. Count up the bars from the left until you pass 25.

hints.text: With $50$ values, the median is the average of the 25th and 26th times in order. Count up the bars from the left until you pass 25.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with bars of $2, 3, 5$ for $10$ values. The median is between the 5th and 6th values. The first two bars hold $2 + 3 = 5$ values, so the 6th is in the third bar. Same counting here.
Running totals: $3$, then $3 + 12 = 15$, then $15 + 20 = 35$. Which bar contains the 25th and 26th values?
Values 16 through 35 are in the $25$ to $<30$ bar, so the 25th and 26th are both there: choice B.

explanation: Order the $50$ times from fastest to slowest. The median sits between the 25th and 26th times.
Cumulative counts: $3$ after the first bar, $15$ after the second, $35$ after the third.
The 25th and 26th times fall in the third bar, $25$ to $<30$ minutes. Choice B. The exact median is unknown, but its bar is certain.

alternativeExplanations.title: Use percents
steps: The median is the 50th percentile, so look for where the cumulative percent crosses 50.
After two bars: $\frac{15}{50} = 30$ percent. After three bars: $\frac{35}{50} = 70$ percent.
Fifty percent is crossed inside the third bar, $25$ to $<30$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why choice D is wrong
steps: A histogram hides the individual times, so you cannot find the exact median.
But it does show how many values are in each bin, and that is enough to locate which bin holds the middle.
So the interval can be determined even though the exact number cannot.

prompt: Priya logged her sleep for five nights: $7, 8, 6, 9$ and $7.5$ hours. What is her mean number of hours of sleep?
hint: The mean shares the total evenly across the nights. What two numbers do you need before you can divide?

hints.text: The mean shares the total evenly across the nights. What two numbers do you need before you can divide?
Add the five nights, $7 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 7.5$, and then divide that total by $5$ because there are five nights.
The total is $37.5$ and $\frac{37.5}{5} = 7.5$, so her mean is $7.5$ hours of sleep.

explanation: The mean is the total amount of sleep divided by the number of nights, so start with the total: $7 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 7.5 = 37.5$ hours.
There are five nights in the log, so the total is divided by $5$.
$\frac{37.5}{5} = 7.5$, so Priya's mean is $7.5$ hours of sleep per night.

alternativeExplanations.title: Balance the deviations
steps: Guess 7.5 and look at the deviations: $-0.5, +0.5, -1.5, +1.5, 0$.
They add to exactly 0, so 7.5 is the balance point — the mean.

prompt: The numbers of text messages six friends sent during lunch were $4, 9, 12, 15, 20, 26$. What is the median?
hint: The median is the middle of an ordered list. With six values, is there a single middle number?

hints.text: The median is the middle of an ordered list. With six values, is there a single middle number?
Six values have two middle positions, the 3rd and 4th, which hold $12$ and $15$. The median is the number halfway between them.
$\frac{12 + 15}{2} = 13.5$, so the median is $13.5$ messages.

explanation: The values $4, 9, 12, 15, 20, 26$ are already in order, which is what the median requires.
With an even count of six there is no single middle value, so use the 3rd and 4th values, $12$ and $15$.
Averaging them gives $\frac{12 + 15}{2} = 13.5$, so the median is $13.5$ messages.

alternativeExplanations.title: Cross off from both ends
steps: Cross off 4 and 26. Cross off 9 and 20.
Two numbers remain, 12 and 15; halfway between them is 13.5.

prompt: The daily high temperatures (°F) in a town one week were $58, 63, 71, 66, 74, 60$ and $69$. What is the range of the temperatures?
hint: The range is one number that tells how far apart the two most extreme values are.

hints.text: The range is one number that tells how far apart the two most extreme values are.
Scan the week for the hottest and the coldest day. They are $74$ and $58$, so subtract the smaller from the larger.
$74 - 58 = 16$, so the range is $16$ degrees Fahrenheit.

explanation: The range only needs the two extremes, so find them: the largest high is $74$ and the smallest is $58$.
Subtract the minimum from the maximum to get the range: $74 - 58 = 16$.
The range of the temperatures is $16$ degrees, a quick measure of spread that depends only on the two extreme days.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sort first
steps: The ends are 58 and 74, so the range is $74 - 58 = 16$.

prompt: Eight students reported how many hours they worked last week: $3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 18$. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
hint: The IQR measures the spread of the middle half of the data. Which two quartiles do you need to find first?

hints.text: The IQR measures the spread of the middle half of the data. Which two quartiles do you need to find first?
Split the ordered list into halves: $3, 5, 7, 8$ and $10, 12, 14, 18$. The median of each half gives $Q_1 = \frac{5 + 7}{2}$ and $Q_3 = \frac{12 + 14}{2}$, and then you subtract.
$Q_1 = 6$ and $Q_3 = 13$, so the IQR is $13 - 6 = 7$ hours.

explanation: With eight ordered values, the lower half is $3, 5, 7, 8$ and the upper half is $10, 12, 14, 18$.
Each quartile is the median of its half, so $Q_1 = \frac{5 + 7}{2} = 6$ and $Q_3 = \frac{12 + 14}{2} = 13$.
The IQR is $Q_3 - Q_1 = 13 - 6 = 7$, so the middle half of the students span $7$ hours.

alternativeExplanations.title: Quartiles as 25th and 75th percentiles
steps: A quarter of the data (2 values) sits below $Q_1$, so $Q_1$ is between the 2nd and 3rd values: between 5 and 7, which is 6.
A quarter sits above $Q_3$, so $Q_3$ is between the 6th and 7th values: between 12 and 14, which is 13.

prompt: For a pizza shop's delivery times, $Q_1 = 20$ minutes and $Q_3 = 32$ minutes. Using the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule, any delivery longer than how many minutes counts as an outlier?
hint: The outlier rule builds a fence above $Q_3$. The distance to the fence depends on the IQR, so that comes first.

hints.text: The outlier rule builds a fence above $Q_3$. The distance to the fence depends on the IQR, so that comes first.
The IQR is $32 - 20 = 12$ minutes. The upper fence sits $1.5 \times 12$ above $Q_3$, so work out $32 + 1.5 \times 12$.
$1.5 \times 12 = 18$ and $32 + 18 = 50$, so any delivery longer than $50$ minutes counts as an outlier.

explanation: The rule measures distance in IQRs, so first find the IQR: $Q_3 - Q_1 = 32 - 20 = 12$ minutes.
The fence lies one and a half IQRs beyond the quartile, and $1.5 \times 12 = 18$ minutes.
The upper fence is $Q_3 + 18 = 32 + 18 = 50$, so deliveries longer than $50$ minutes are outliers.

alternativeExplanations.title: Both fences at once
steps: Lower fence: $20 - 18 = 2$ minutes. Upper fence: $32 + 18 = 50$ minutes.
The "normal" window is 2 to 50 minutes; anything outside is an outlier.
The question asks about long deliveries, so the answer is the upper fence, 50.

prompt: Five plants in a science class are $1, 3, 5, 7$ and $9$ cm tall. What is the sample standard deviation of the heights? Round to two decimal places.
hint: Standard deviation describes the typical distance of the values from their mean, so the mean is the place to start.

hints.text: Standard deviation describes the typical distance of the values from their mean, so the mean is the place to start.
The mean is $5$, so the deviations are $-4, -2, 0, 2, 4$. Square them, add the squares, divide by $n - 1 = 4$, and take the square root.
The squares add to $40$, $\frac{40}{4} = 10$, and $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$, so the sample standard deviation is about $3.16$ cm.

explanation: Deviations are measured from the mean, which is $\frac{1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9}{5} = 5$ cm.
The deviations $-4, -2, 0, 2, 4$ are squared so that negatives do not cancel positives: $16, 4, 0, 4, 16$, which sum to $40$.
For a sample, divide by $n - 1$ rather than $n$, so the variance is $\frac{40}{4} = 10$.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so $s = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$ cm.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why divide by 4 and not 5
steps: These five plants are a sample, and dividing by $n - 1$ makes the sample variance an unbiased estimate of the population variance.
Dividing by 5 would give $\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$, the population SD — a different (and here, wrong) answer.
AP Statistics uses $s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$ for sample data: 3.16.

prompt: A boxplot of the pages read by a book club last month has five-number summary $12, 18, 24, 31, 40$ (min, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, max). What percent of the members read between $18$ and $31$ pages?
hint: $18$ is $Q_1$ and $31$ is $Q_3$. Those are the edges of the BOX.

hints.text: $18$ is $Q_1$ and $31$ is $Q_3$. Those are the edges of the BOX.
The box always holds the middle half of the data, no matter how wide or narrow it looks.
From $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ is $50$ percent of the members.

explanation: $Q_1 = 18$ has about $25$ percent of the data below it; $Q_3 = 31$ has about $75$ percent below it.
Between them lies $75 - 25 = 50$ percent of the data.
So about $50$ percent of the members read between $18$ and $31$ pages.

alternativeExplanations.title: Four equal pieces
steps: The five-number summary cuts the data into four quarters: 12 to 18, 18 to 24, 24 to 31 and 31 to 40.
Each piece holds 25 percent of the members, even though the pieces are different widths.
18 to 31 covers two pieces: $25 + 25 = 50$ percent.

prompt: A weather station's daily highs in Celsius have mean $20$ and standard deviation $4$. The data are converted to Fahrenheit using $F = 1.8C + 32$. What is the standard deviation of the Fahrenheit temperatures?
hint: The conversion does two things to each temperature: it multiplies and it adds. Think about which of those changes how spread out the values are.

hints.text: The conversion does two things to each temperature: it multiplies and it adds. Think about which of those changes how spread out the values are.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with the values $1, 3$, which have SD $\sqrt{2}$. Add $10$ to get $11, 13$ and the SD stays the same. Double them to get $2, 6$ and the SD doubles. Multiplying stretches spread; adding does not.
Adding $32$ shifts every day equally, so it leaves the spread alone. Only the multiplier matters: multiply the Celsius standard deviation $4$ by $1.8$.
$1.8 \times 4 = 7.2$, so the standard deviation is $7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit.

explanation: For a linear change $y = a + bx$, the mean becomes $a + b\bar{x}$ but the standard deviation becomes $|b| \cdot s_x$.
The $+32$ moves every day by the same amount, so the distances between values, and therefore the spread, are untouched.
The multiplier $1.8$ stretches every distance by $1.8$, so $s_F = 1.8 \times 4 = 7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit. (The mean becomes $1.8(20) + 32 = 68$.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Follow two actual days
steps: A day at $20^\circ$C converts to $68^\circ$F. A day one SD warmer, $24^\circ$C, converts to $1.8(24) + 32 = 75.2^\circ$F.
The gap was 4 degrees Celsius and is now $75.2 - 68 = 7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit.
Every gap stretches by 1.8, so the SD does too: 7.2.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap: adding 32 to the SD
steps: It is tempting to compute $1.8(4) + 32 = 39.2$. That is what happens to the MEAN, not the SD.
Spread measures distances between values, and sliding everything up by 32 leaves every distance alone.
So only the multiplier matters for the SD: $7.2$.

prompt: A realtor lists the prices of $10$ homes. The most expensive home is then relisted at DOUBLE its price, and nothing else changes. Which statistics must change?

choices.label: The mean and the standard deviation
All four: mean, median, SD and IQR
None of them, because only one value changed

hint: Resistant statistics depend on the POSITION of values in order, not their exact size. Non-resistant ones add up every value.

hints.text: Resistant statistics depend on the POSITION of values in order, not their exact size. Non-resistant ones add up every value.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. Change the $5$ to $50$. The median stays $3$ and the quartiles stay $1.5$ and $4.5$, but the mean jumps from $3$ to $12$. Same logic with 10 prices.
The biggest price is still the biggest after doubling, so the ordered list has the same 5th, 6th and quartile positions. Which statistics use the actual dollar amounts of every home?
The mean and SD use every value, so both increase. Median and IQR stay put. Choice A.

explanation: The doubled price is still the maximum, so the order of the homes does not change. The median (average of the 5th and 6th prices) and the quartiles are unchanged, so the IQR is unchanged.
The mean adds every price, so it rises. The SD measures distance from the mean, and the new maximum sits much farther out, so the SD rises too.
Mean and SD change; median and IQR do not. Choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: Resistant vs non-resistant
steps: Median and IQR are resistant: they shrug off extreme values.
Mean and SD are non-resistant: one extreme value can swing them a lot.
This is why the AP exam says to pair median with IQR for skewed data, and mean with SD for roughly symmetric data.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice D
steps: "Only one value changed" sounds like a small change, but doubling the largest price is a huge change in dollars.
Any statistic that uses that dollar amount, like the mean, must move.
So D is false; only the position-based statistics stay fixed.

prompt: The weights (pounds) of nine dogs at a shelter are $14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 38$. Using the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule, what is the upper fence for outliers?
